opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, partly because of my background. I came up through computational neuroscience, and if you look at how the brain is actually allocated, a huge fraction of cortex is devoted to visual processing in one way or another. We're fundamentally visual animals. Language is this incredibly recent add-on, evolutionarily speaking. It's maybe a hundred thousand years old, give or take, and writing is only a few thousand years old. So there's something a little funny about the fact that the technology that's taking off right now is text-in, text-out.

But I don't think that undercuts the usefulness of LLMs for knowledge work. I actually think it points to why they're so useful. Most knowledge work has already been squeezed through the bottleneck of language and symbols. When you write code, write a legal brief, analyze a spreadsheet, or write a paper, you've already taken all that rich perceptual and intuitive understanding and compressed it into a linear stream of tokens. That's the medium knowledge work lives in. So models that are extremely good at manipulating that medium plug directly into where the work is happening.

Where I think the visual bias really shows up is on the human side of the interface. People don't want to read a wall of text. When you're reviewing what an agent did, or trying to understand a complex system, you want diagrams, plots, dashboards, something you can take in at a glance. Our visual system is extraordinarily high bandwidth and our reading is comparatively slow and serial. So I think a lot of the opportunity right now is in closing that gap: letting the model do the heavy lifting in language and code, and then rendering the results back in a form that fits how our brains actually want to consume information. Think generated visualizations, interactive artifacts, UIs that the model builds on the fly.

And then there's the other direction, which is the models themselves getting better at vision. They're improving fast, but there's still a gap between how well they reason over text and how well they reason over, say, a messy screenshot or a scientific figure. As that closes, a lot of knowledge work that's implicitly visual, like reading charts, navigating interfaces, or looking at experimental data, becomes much more accessible to them.

So my short answer is that language is the compression format of knowledge work, which is why LLMs are so powerful there. But the last mile to the human is visual, and I think that's where a lot of the interesting product and research work is going to be over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says knowledge work is compressed into language and symbols, but does not observe that these activities are ones humans did not evolve to perform.

r002.rationale: It says a huge fraction of the cortex is devoted to visual processing and describes language as evolutionarily recent, tentatively conveying greater brain allocation to vision than language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at something people underrate about why these tools are so weird to use. A huge fraction of our brain is devoted to vision. We've had hundreds of millions of years of evolution tuning that machinery, and when you look at a spreadsheet or a dashboard or a diagram, you're parsing a very dense amount of information almost for free. Language is comparatively recent and comparatively low bandwidth. Reading is slow, writing is slow, and it's a serial channel.

So when you hand someone a model that lives almost entirely in text, you're forcing a lot of knowledge work through a narrow pipe. I think that's actually one of the reasons adoption in real workflows has been bumpier than the benchmarks would suggest. The model might be perfectly capable, but the interface is a chat box, and a chat box is a bad way to look at a thousand things at once.

That said, I'd push back on the idea that this makes the models less useful. It changes where they're useful. The value isn't in the model replacing your visual intuition about a problem. It's in the model doing the long, boring, serial work that we're bad at and don't enjoy. Reading forty documents, cross-referencing them, drafting the first version of something, running the search you'd never get around to running. Those are things where our vision doesn't help us much anyway.

And then the interesting design problem is on the output side. If the model's work gets handed back to you as a wall of text, you're stuck in the slow channel again. If it gets handed back as something you can see, a plot, a table, a diff, a structured view where the anomaly pops out, you're back on the evolutionary fast path. So I think the real leverage is in pairing them. Let the model do the reading and the writing, and let the human do the looking. A lot of the best tooling I've seen is basically that: the model does a bunch of serial labor and then compresses it into something your visual cortex can eat in two seconds.

The models are also getting better at vision themselves, which closes part of the gap from the other direction. But even then, I think the human-in-the-loop version keeps looking like this for a while. We're the ones with the ridiculously good eyes. The model is the thing that doesn't get bored.

r001.rationale: The response describes serial knowledge work as boring and difficult for humans, but does not say that modern knowledge work involves activities humans did not evolve to perform.

r002.rationale: It says a huge fraction of the brain is devoted to vision and contrasts vision with language as a more recent, lower-bandwidth channel, conveying that vision receives greater brain investment.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between how we take in the world and how we communicate about it. Vision is an enormous part of how humans navigate their environment, but a lot of knowledge work happens through language. We write documents, exchange messages, read research, and explain decisions. So a system that can work with language has access to a very useful part of that process, even if it doesn’t perceive the world the way we do.

But language isn’t the whole thing. Sometimes you look at a chart or a sketch and immediately see a relationship that would take several paragraphs to explain. I’d want these tools to work across those representations—to help you move from a description to something you can inspect visually, and then discuss what you see.

So I don’t think our bias toward vision makes LLMs less useful. I think it tells us something about how to use them. A conversational interface is useful for some tasks, but it shouldn’t have to be the interface for every task.

r001.rationale: The response says much knowledge work happens through language, but does not observe that these are activities humans did not evolve to perform.

r002.rationale: It describes vision as an enormous part of navigating the environment, but makes no claim about brain tissue allocation relative to language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a temptation to equate how much of our brain is devoted to something with how economically useful that thing is. Vision is incredibly important to humans, but a lot of knowledge work happens through language. We write documents, read papers, send emails, write code. So a system that works primarily with language can still be useful across a huge fraction of what people do at a computer.

The other distinction is between doing the whole job and helping with parts of it. An LLM doesn’t need to perceive the world the way you do to help you draft something or work through an argument. You can supply the context and judge the result. That doesn’t mean vision is irrelevant—it matters a lot for some tasks—but I wouldn’t take our evolutionary investment in vision as a ceiling on how useful language models can be.

r001.rationale: The response says much knowledge work happens through language and lists documents, papers, email, and code, but it does not state that these are activities humans did not evolve to perform.
